invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

# FIG. 2

A flat schematic diagram of one connector channel in plain black line work on white, no shading and no text inside the drawing area. All line work stays well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.

A dashed rectangle occupies the left and central portion of the drawing area, representing the first connector channel.

A solid vertical line enters from above, crosses the top side of the dashed rectangle and continues downward inside it, as the incoming branch supply. Inside the dashed rectangle this line is interrupted by a contactor, shown schematically as a small empty square outline straddling the line, the line meeting the outline above and below.

Below the contactor the line resumes, turns right and runs horizontally to the right side of the dashed rectangle. A small square outline straddles this horizontal run and represents the connector current sensor, shown schematically, the run continuing to the right of it.

An empty rectangular block sits in the lower region of the dashed rectangle, below the horizontal run, representing the control-pilot interface.

Where the horizontal run reaches the right side of the dashed rectangle it meets an empty rectangular block straddling that side, the vehicle connector, shown schematically.

Right of the dashed rectangle a larger rounded rectangle represents an electric vehicle, shown schematically. A short solid line runs from the right side of the vehicle connector block to the left side of the rounded rectangle. A second solid line runs from the right side of the control-pilot interface block to the lower side of the vehicle connector block.

A solid horizontal line enters from the left and crosses the left side of the dashed rectangle in its lower region, representing the isolated local bus. Inside the dashed rectangle it branches three ways: one branch reaches the left side of the control-pilot interface block, a second runs upward and reaches the contactor outline, and a third runs upward and reaches the square outline representing the connector current sensor.

The part names listed below are semantic identifiers only and do not appear as drawing text.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 108 isolated local bus: leader ends on the bus line left of the dashed rectangle.
- 120 first connector channel: leader ends on the dashed rectangle.
- 122 contactor: leader ends on the square outline straddling the vertical line.
- 124 connector current sensor: leader ends on the square outline straddling the horizontal run.
- 126 control-pilot interface: leader ends well inside the block in the lower region of the dashed rectangle.
- 128 vehicle connector: leader ends well inside the block straddling the right side.
- 130 electric vehicle: leader ends well inside the rounded rectangle.

Both parts of the single verified finding are fixed, and I checked the rest of the draft for the same assertion.

**Changes:**

- `draft/07-drawings.md` still matches FIG. 2 (it names the contactor, connector current sensor, control-pilot interface and vehicle connector, none of which changed).
- Remaining bus mentions (`draft/08` paragraphs 7, 15 and 23, FIG-1 line 17, FIG-3 line 17) reach only the connector channels as wholes, the control-pilot interfaces and the contactors, so nothing else asserts a sensor on the bus.
- `draft/numerals.md` unchanged: 108 still has exactly one part name and appears in FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 only.

input.summary: Removed the unsupported assertion that the isolated local bus carries connector current sensor reports, in both the detailed description and the FIG. 2 brief, and verified that the numeral table, drawing descriptions, claims and remaining figure briefs stay synchronized.
reasoning: The single verified finding was a scope leak, not a claim problem. The only source sentence about the bus is "A controller communicates with the connector interfaces and contactors over an isolated local bus," which names the control-pilot interfaces and the contactors and nothing else. Paragraph 7 of the detailed description had added the connector current sensor reports to that list, and the FIG. 2 brief had verbalized a matching third bus branch. Both were removed; nothing was added anywhere to compensate.

A bus branch to a named component is a topology assertion, so I treated it as substance rather than as a depiction convention and deleted the branch from the brief rather than trying to justify it as schematic. The connector current sensor itself stays in FIG. 2, straddling the horizontal run downstream of the contactor, because that placement is required by the disclosed reclosure test (zero connector current after an open command) and by welded-contactor detection.

Claim 5 was already the narrower and supported statement, reciting the bus as coupling the controller to the control-pilot interfaces and the contactors only. I left it and every other claim untouched, so the description now sits within the claim it supports instead of outside it, which is the direction that keeps written-description support intact.

FIG. 1 needed no change: its bus branches rise to the connector channel blocks as wholes, and a channel contains both the control-pilot interface and the contactor, so that depiction never asserted a sensor connection. FIG. 3 likewise shows only a single connection leaving the controller toward the branch current sensor and the bus.

I confirmed the sensor numeral 124 is still drawn and still listed on FIG. 2, so removing the branch did not orphan a numeral or leave a listed part without a visible target, and the Brief Description of the Drawings still matches each brief without edit.
